name: MDS210 SA1 Mock Exam
subtitle: Structure of Cell, Basic Tissue, Protein Sorting, Embryogenesis, Cell Signaling
description: 60-question mock exam covering LEC 1-5 (Structure & Function of Cell Components, Structure & Function of Basic Tissue, Protein Sorting & Vesicular Transport, Embryogenesis & Stem Cells, Cell Signaling), question count weighted by lecture hours per the course syllabus (10 questions per lecture hour).

questions.stem: Which best describes the distribution of phospholipids in a typical plasma membrane?
options: Phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin are enriched in the outer leaflet
Phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin are enriched in the inner leaflet
Phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine are enriched in the outer leaflet
All phospholipid types are distributed equally between the two leaflets
Cholesterol determines which leaflet each phospholipid occupies
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane is asymmetric: choline-containing phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin) predominate in the outer leaflet, while phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine are concentrated in the inner (cytosolic) leaflet.

questions.stem: A researcher progressively adds cholesterol to an artificial phospholipid bilayer at physiological temperature. What is the most likely effect on the membrane?
options: Increased fluidity and increased permeability to water
Decreased fluidity and increased mechanical strength
Complete loss of the bilayer structure
Conversion of the bilayer into a lipid raft only
No measurable change in membrane properties
questions.explanation: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipid tails, restricting their movement at physiological temperature. This decreases fluidity while increasing the mechanical stability of the membrane, the classic 'fluidity buffer' role of cholesterol.

questions.stem: Which class of membrane protein is anchored to the bilayer without any part of the polypeptide chain entering the hydrophobic core, being attached instead via a covalently linked lipid group?
questions.explanation: Lipid-anchored proteins (e.g., GPI-anchored proteins, G-protein alpha subunits) are tethered to the membrane surface by a covalently attached lipid tail rather than spanning the bilayer, distinguishing them from transmembrane and peripheral proteins.

questions.stem: A nuclear structure is spherical, has no surrounding membrane, and disappears during mitosis before reforming in telophase. Its principal function is:
options: Ribosomal RNA synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly
questions.explanation: This describes the nucleolus, a non-membrane-bound, electron-dense nuclear structure responsible for transcribing rRNA genes and assembling ribosomal subunits.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes mitochondria from the other cytoplasmic organelles listed?
options: Is the primary site of protein glycosylation
Contains its own circular DNA and can self-replicate
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are unique among these organelles in possessing their own DNA (consistent with an endosymbiotic origin) and undergoing independent self-replication, in addition to being double-membraned with cristae for oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.stem: Which cell type would be expected to show the most extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic acinar cells are specialized for synthesis and secretion of large quantities of digestive enzymes, requiring abundant RER for co-translational protein synthesis and translocation into the ER lumen.

questions.stem: Chronic alcohol use is associated with proliferation of which organelle in hepatocytes, reflecting its role in detoxification?
questions.explanation: The smooth ER contains cytochrome P450 enzymes that detoxify alcohol and other lipid-soluble drugs; chronic exposure induces SER proliferation in hepatocytes.

questions.stem: The convex (cis) face of the Golgi apparatus is functionally defined by which of the following?
options: It is the site where mature secretory vesicles bud off toward the plasma membrane
It is the site of lysosomal enzyme phosphorylation exclusively
It receives transport vesicles arriving from the rough endoplasmic reticulum
It contains the highest concentration of acid hydrolases
It is continuous with the nuclear envelope
questions.explanation: The cis-Golgi network is the 'receiving' face, accepting ER-derived transport vesicles; the trans-Golgi network is the 'shipping' face from which mature vesicles depart to their final destinations.

questions.stem: A child presents with progressive neurodegeneration and a cherry-red spot on retinal exam. Enzyme testing reveals deficiency of hexosaminidase A, with abnormal accumulation of GM2 ganglioside. Which organelle is primarily dysfunctional?
questions.explanation: This describes Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient hexosaminidase A activity, so that the lysosome cannot degrade GM2 ganglioside.

questions.stem: Deficiency of catalase within a specific organelle would most directly impair the breakdown of which molecule?
questions.explanation: Catalase is the major peroxisomal enzyme; it converts the hydrogen peroxide generated by peroxisomal oxidase reactions into water and oxygen, preventing accumulation of this reactive oxygen species.

questions.stem: Which feature is common to all types of epithelial tissue?
options: Structural and functional polarity between apical and basal surfaces
Rich vascular supply within the epithelial layer itself
Loose arrangement of cells with abundant extracellular space
questions.explanation: All epithelia are polarized, tightly packed, avascular, sit on a basement membrane, and can regenerate; polarity between the apical and basal surfaces is a universal defining feature.

questions.stem: Simple squamous epithelium lining the peritoneal, pleural, and pericardial cavities is specifically termed:
questions.explanation: Mesothelium is the simple squamous epithelium lining body cavities (peritoneum, pleura, pericardium); endothelium is the analogous lining of blood and lymphatic vessels.

questions.stem: A tissue sample shows a single layer of cells, all resting on the basement membrane, but with nuclei at different apparent heights, giving a false impression of stratification; cilia are present at the apical surface. This best describes:
questions.explanation: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is a single cell layer in which not every cell reaches the free surface, so nuclei appear at varying levels; it lines the respiratory tract and is typically ciliated.

questions.stem: Which epithelial type is best suited to line an organ that must withstand large changes in volume, such as the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) has cells that can flatten and slide over one another, allowing the epithelium to stretch considerably as the bladder fills.

questions.stem: Microvilli on the apical surface of absorptive epithelial cells contain a core supported mainly by:
options: Tubulin dimers arranged as a 9+2 axoneme
questions.explanation: Each microvillus is supported by a core bundle of actin microfilaments, cross-linked by proteins such as fimbrin and villin, distinct from the microtubule-based axoneme of cilia.

questions.stem: Unusually long, immotile microvilli found lining the epididymis and ductus deferens are termed:
questions.explanation: Stereocilia are elongated, non-motile microvilli (actin-cored, despite the name) found in the epididymis/ductus deferens and in the inner ear sensory epithelium.

questions.stem: A secretory cell releases its product by pinching off apical cytoplasm together with the secretory material, so that a portion of the cell is lost with each release event. This mode of secretion is:
questions.explanation: Apocrine secretion involves loss of a small portion of apical cytoplasm along with the secretory product, in contrast to merocrine (exocytosis only, no cell loss) and holocrine (whole-cell disintegration, e.g., sebaceous gland).

questions.stem: A gland has a single, unbranched excretory duct and a secretory portion arranged as a single flask-shaped (rounded) unit. This is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: A simple acinar gland has one unbranched duct draining a single rounded (acinar) secretory unit, distinguishing it from tubular glands (elongated secretory portion) and compound glands (branched duct system).

questions.stem: Which histologic feature distinguishes a serous secretory cell from a mucous secretory cell under light microscopy?
options: Serous cells have a foamy, pale-staining cytoplasm
Mucous cells have abundant RER and eosinophilic cytoplasm
Serous cells lack secretory granules entirely
Serous cells have a rounded, basally located nucleus and basophilic cytoplasm rich in RER
Mucous cells have a narrower lumen than serous cells
questions.explanation: Serous cells (e.g., parotid, pancreatic acinar) have round, basally placed nuclei and basophilic cytoplasm from abundant RER, secreting a thin, protein-rich fluid, in contrast to mucous cells, which appear pale/foamy with flattened, basally pushed nuclei.

questions.stem: The submandibular salivary gland is classified as a compound gland with mixed secretory units because it contains:
options: Only serous acini arranged in a branched tubular pattern
Only mucous tubules with no serous component
Mucous tubules capped by crescent-shaped serous demilunes
questions.explanation: The submandibular (and sublingual) gland is a mixed seromucous gland: mucous tubular units are capped by serous 'demilunes,' crescent-shaped clusters of serous cells, giving both watery and viscous secretions.

questions.stem: A ribosome begins translating an mRNA in the cytosol. As the nascent polypeptide emerges, a hydrophobic ER signal sequence is recognized by a cytosolic ribonucleoprotein particle, which pauses translation and escorts the ribosome-mRNA complex to the ER membrane. This particle is the:
questions.explanation: The signal recognition particle (SRP) binds the emerging ER signal sequence, pauses translation, and delivers the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the SRP receptor on the rough ER membrane, initiating cotranslational translocation.

questions.stem: Proteins synthesized entirely on free ribosomes in the cytosol, which never enter the endoplasmic reticulum, can be post-translationally imported into which of the following destinations?
questions.explanation: Proteins made on free (cytosolic) ribosomes either remain in the cytosol or are post-translationally imported into mitochondria, peroxisomes, or the nucleus, organelles reached without passing through the ER-Golgi pathway.

questions.stem: A soluble luminal protein that must remain permanently within the endoplasmic reticulum carries which carboxy-terminal sequence to prevent its escape into the secretory pathway?
questions.explanation: The KDEL (Lys-Asp-Glu-Leu) sequence at the C-terminus is recognized by the KDEL receptor in the cis-Golgi/ERGIC, which returns escaped ER-resident proteins to the ER via COPI-coated retrograde vesicles.

questions.stem: Which coat protein is primarily responsible for anterograde transport of newly synthesized cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum toward the Golgi apparatus?
questions.explanation: COPII-coated vesicles bud from ER exit sites and mediate forward (anterograde) transport of cargo from the ER to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and cis-Golgi; COPI mediates the reverse (retrograde) direction.

questions.stem: Retrieval of escaped ER-resident proteins and recycling of Golgi-resident enzymes back to earlier Golgi cisternae is primarily mediated by which coated vesicle type?
questions.explanation: COPI-coated vesicles mediate retrograde transport, from the Golgi back to the ER and between Golgi cisternae, complementing the forward transport carried out by COPII vesicles.

questions.stem: Newly synthesized lysosomal hydrolases are tagged in the cis-Golgi by addition of which molecule, allowing recognition by a dedicated receptor for lysosomal sorting?
questions.explanation: A phosphotransferase in the cis-Golgi adds phosphate to mannose residues on lysosomal hydrolases, generating mannose-6-phosphate (M6P). The M6P receptor in the trans-Golgi network then packages these enzymes into vesicles destined for the lysosome.

questions.stem: Specificity of vesicle fusion with the correct target membrane is largely explained by complementary pairing between:
options: v-SNAREs on the vesicle and t-SNAREs on the target membrane
Signal peptidase and the signal sequence
questions.explanation: The SNARE hypothesis proposes that a vesicle-associated SNARE (v-SNARE, e.g., synaptobrevin) pairs specifically with a target-membrane SNARE (t-SNARE, e.g., syntaxin/SNAP-25), forming a tight complex that drives and directs membrane fusion.

questions.stem: A bacterial toxin cleaves synaptobrevin (a v-SNARE) at the presynaptic terminal, preventing fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles with the plasma membrane and causing acute flaccid paralysis. This mechanism describes:
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin is a zinc-dependent protease that cleaves SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction, blocking acetylcholine release and producing flaccid paralysis.

questions.stem: Following retrograde axonal transport to the central nervous system, a related bacterial toxin cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory interneurons, blocking release of glycine and GABA and causing sustained, unopposed excitation of motor neurons. This describes the mechanism of:
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxin is transported retrogradely to the spinal cord, where it cleaves SNARE proteins in inhibitory neurons, preventing release of glycine and GABA. Loss of inhibition causes sustained motor neuron firing and spastic paralysis (lockjaw).

questions.stem: LDL particles are internalized by hepatocytes after binding the LDL receptor, which clusters into a specialized region of the plasma membrane before internalization within a coated vesicle. Which protein coats this vesicle?
questions.explanation: LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis proceeds through clathrin-coated pits: LDL binds its receptor, the complex clusters into a clathrin-coated pit, and the pit buds inward as a clathrin-coated vesicle that fuses with an endosome.

questions.stem: Before a sperm can fertilize an oocyte, it must undergo a series of membrane changes in the female reproductive tract that remove glycoproteins from the sperm head, a process termed:
questions.explanation: Capacitation occurs in the female reproductive tract and involves removal of glycoproteins and cholesterol from the sperm plasma membrane, a step that must precede the acrosome reaction.

questions.stem: Immediately after a single sperm fuses with the oocyte plasma membrane, cortical granules release their contents into the perivitelline space, modifying the zona pellucida. The primary purpose of this cortical reaction is to:
options: Determine the sex of the embryo
questions.explanation: The cortical reaction alters the zona pellucida to block additional sperm from penetrating, ensuring only one sperm fertilizes the oocyte and preventing polyspermy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct outcome of fertilization?
options: Formation of the trophoblast and inner cell mass
Determination of embryo sex, restoration of the diploid number, and initiation of cleavage
questions.explanation: The three principal results of fertilization are restoration of the diploid chromosome number, determination of genetic sex, and initiation of the mitotic cleavage divisions that produce the blastomeres.

questions.stem: At the blastocyst stage, the outer cell layer that will give rise to the fetal contribution of the placenta is the:
questions.explanation: The blastocyst separates into an outer trophoblast, which forms the placenta (cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast), and an inner cell mass (embryoblast), which forms the embryo proper.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with severe right lower quadrant pain, slight vaginal bleeding, and a missed period roughly 8 weeks prior. Serum hCG is low relative to expected gestational age. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Low or plateauing hCG together with unilateral pain and bleeding around 6-8 weeks is classic for ectopic (commonly tubal) pregnancy; a molar pregnancy instead produces markedly elevated hCG.

questions.stem: Erosion of the syncytiotrophoblast into maternal endometrial vessels, forming blood-filled lacunae, first occurs during:
options: Implantation is complete before any lacunae form
questions.explanation: During the second week, the syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium, and lacunae develop within it that fill with maternal blood, establishing the earliest uteroplacental circulation.

questions.stem: A hydatidiform mole is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Presence of a normally developing fetus alongside abnormal placental tissue
Very high serum hCG relative to gestational age
Vaginal bleeding often described as prune-juice colored
Grape-like clusters of villi seen on ultrasound
questions.explanation: A hydatidiform mole shows abnormal, cystic placental tissue with grape-like villi, marked hCG elevation, and vaginal bleeding, but is defined by the absence of a viable fetus; the trophoblast proliferates without normal embryonic development.

questions.stem: The process by which epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three definitive germ layers is called:
questions.explanation: Gastrulation is the process, beginning with formation of the primitive streak in the third week, by which epiblast cells migrate to establish the trilaminar germ disc: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

questions.stem: The notochord, formed from cells migrating cranially from the primitive node, is critical for early development because it:
options: Gives rise to the neural crest
Induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate
questions.explanation: The notochord provides the inductive signal that causes the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, initiating neurulation; it does not itself become the vertebral bodies, persisting only as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

questions.stem: Failure of the neural tube to close properly by the end of the fourth week is most strongly associated with a maternal deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Adequate maternal folic acid intake around conception is critical for normal neural tube closure; deficiency significantly raises the risk of defects such as spina bifida or anencephaly.

questions.stem: Which set of germ layer derivatives is correctly matched?
options: Neural crest to adrenal medulla and melanocytes
questions.explanation: Neural crest cells give rise to structures including the adrenal medulla, melanocytes, dorsal root ganglia, and Schwann cells; the notochord does not become the vertebral bodies, and the epidermis is a surface ectoderm derivative, not endoderm.

questions.stem: During embryonic folding in the fourth week, formation of the foregut and repositioning of the developing heart and septum transversum ventrally is driven primarily by:
questions.explanation: Head folding brings the developing brain to the most cranial position, forms the foregut, and rotates the primordial heart, septum transversum, and oropharyngeal membrane into a ventral position.

questions.stem: Which extraembryonic membrane becomes incorporated into the hindgut during folding and later forms the fetal urachus?
questions.explanation: The allantois, a diverticulum from the caudal yolk sac, becomes incorporated into the hindgut during folding and later forms the urachus, connecting the fetal bladder to the umbilical region; it obliterates by the 12th week to become the median umbilical ligament.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is found to have an amniotic fluid volume greater than 2000 mL (polyhydramnios). Which mechanism most directly explains this finding?
options: Decreased absorption of amniotic fluid, such as with fetal inability to swallow
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios most often results from decreased absorption/swallowing of amniotic fluid (e.g., esophageal atresia, anencephaly impairing swallowing), whereas oligohydramnios classically results from decreased production, such as with renal agenesis reducing fetal urine output.

questions.stem: Amniocentesis is generally performed at approximately which gestational age, in part to allow adequate amniotic fluid volume for safe sampling?
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis is typically performed at 14-16 weeks of gestation, when sufficient amniotic fluid volume is present, allowing karyotyping of cultured fetal cells and measurement of substances such as alpha-fetoprotein.

questions.stem: Which finding on amniocentesis is most suggestive of a fetal neural tube defect?
questions.explanation: Open neural tube defects allow leakage of fetal serum proteins, including alpha-fetoprotein, into the amniotic fluid, so elevated amniotic AFP is a classic marker for conditions such as spina bifida or anencephaly.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the fetal contribution to the definitive placenta?
questions.explanation: The chorion frondosum (villous chorion), the region of chorion with well-developed, vascularized villi, forms the fetal part of the placenta; the decidua basalis is the corresponding maternal contribution.

questions.stem: Monozygotic twins resulting from splitting of the inner cell mass, in which the two embryos share a single chorion but have separate amniotic sacs, are described as:
questions.explanation: When monozygotic twinning occurs after the chorion has formed but before the amnion has formed, the twins share a single chorion but develop separate amniotic sacs, the most common pattern for monozygotic twins.

questions.stem: A population of stem cells can differentiate into a limited number of closely related cell types but is not capable of forming all tissues of an organ system. This describes:
questions.explanation: Multipotent stem cells, such as hematopoietic stem cells that give rise to the various blood cell lineages, differentiate into multiple related cell types within a lineage but, unlike pluripotent stem cells, cannot form all cell types of the body.

questions.stem: Adult somatic cells that have been reprogrammed in the laboratory by introducing genes controlling pluripotency, generating cells with properties similar to embryonic stem cells, are called:
questions.explanation: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are generated by reprogramming adult somatic cells with core pluripotency-associated genes, producing cells that behave similarly to embryonic stem cells without requiring an embryo.

questions.stem: Cell-surface receptors are classified into four major categories based on their signaling mechanism. Which pairing of receptor with its correct category is accurate?
options: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) receptor - ligand-gated ion channel
questions.explanation: The beta-adrenergic receptor is a classic G protein-coupled (metabotropic) receptor. The insulin receptor is actually a catalytic receptor tyrosine kinase; GABA-A and nicotinic ACh receptors are ligand-gated ion channels; the ANP receptor is a catalytic receptor guanylyl cyclase, not a channel.

questions.stem: Binding of acetylcholine to the nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction opens a non-selective cation channel. The predominant immediate effect on the postsynaptic membrane potential is:
options: Hyperpolarization due to K+ efflux exceeding Na+ influx
Depolarization due to Na+ influx exceeding K+ efflux
No change, since the channel is equally permeable to Na+ and K+
questions.explanation: Although the nicotinic receptor channel conducts both Na+ and K+, the electrochemical driving force for Na+ influx is much larger than for K+ efflux, so the net effect is depolarization, producing an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP).

questions.stem: Opening of the GABA-A receptor channel produces an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) primarily because it is selectively permeable to:
questions.explanation: The GABA-A receptor is a ligand-gated chloride channel; GABA binding opens the channel, allowing Cl- influx that hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane, producing an IPSP.

questions.stem: In the classic model of G protein-coupled receptor activation, binding of an agonist to the receptor causes the alpha subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein to:
options: Exchange bound GDP for GTP and dissociate from the beta-gamma subunits
questions.explanation: Agonist binding to a GPCR promotes exchange of GDP for GTP on the G-alpha subunit. The GTP-bound alpha subunit dissociates from the beta-gamma dimer, and both can regulate downstream effectors until intrinsic GTPase activity hydrolyzes GTP back to GDP, terminating the signal.

questions.stem: A stimulatory G protein (Gs) activates adenylyl cyclase, while an inhibitory G protein (Gi) has the opposite effect on the same enzyme. This difference in effect on a shared target is due to:
options: Gs and Gi using entirely different second messengers
Gi lacking a beta-gamma subunit entirely
Gs requiring calcium as a cofactor while Gi does not
Gi binding only to nuclear receptors
Differences in the specific alpha subunit each G protein contains
questions.explanation: Gs and Gi are distinguished by their distinct G-alpha subunits: Gs-alpha stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP, while Gi-alpha inhibits adenylyl cyclase to lower cAMP, allowing the same enzyme to be regulated in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Cyclic AMP generated by adenylyl cyclase exerts most of its intracellular effects by activating:
questions.explanation: cAMP is the principal activator of cAMP-dependent protein kinase, or protein kinase A (PKA), which then phosphorylates downstream target proteins to produce the cellular response.

questions.stem: Activation of a Gq-coupled receptor leads to phospholipase C-mediated hydrolysis of PIP2 into two second messengers. Which pairing of second messenger with its downstream action is correct?
options: IP3 activates protein kinase C directly
IP3 triggers calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum, while DAG activates protein kinase C
Diacylglycerol (DAG) opens calcium channels on the endoplasmic reticulum
Both IP3 and DAG activate adenylyl cyclase
IP3 and DAG are functionally interchangeable
questions.explanation: Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into IP3, which diffuses to the ER and opens calcium channels to release Ca2+ into the cytosol, and DAG, which remains in the membrane and activates protein kinase C (PKC), often together with the released calcium.

questions.stem: Cholera toxin produces its dramatic secretory diarrhea by covalently modifying the alpha subunit of Gs in intestinal epithelial cells in a way that:
options: Increases the intrinsic GTPase activity of Gs, rapidly terminating signaling
Prevents Gs from ever binding GTP
Locks Gs in its active, GTP-bound state by inhibiting its GTPase activity
Converts Gs into an inhibitory G protein
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs alpha subunit, inhibiting its intrinsic GTPase activity. Gs is therefore locked in the active GTP-bound state, causing persistent stimulation of adenylyl cyclase, sustained high intracellular cAMP, and massive chloride/water secretion into the gut lumen.

questions.stem: The insulin receptor and the receptor for epidermal growth factor (EGF) both belong to which class of cell-surface receptor?
questions.explanation: Insulin and EGF receptors are receptor tyrosine kinases, a subclass of enzyme-linked (catalytic) receptors that autophosphorylate tyrosine residues upon ligand binding to initiate downstream signaling cascades.

questions.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) binds a membrane receptor with intrinsic guanylyl cyclase activity. The resulting rise in intracellular cGMP activates which downstream kinase to mediate ANP's effects, such as inhibition of renal sodium and water reabsorption?
questions.explanation: ANP receptor activation generates cGMP via guanylyl cyclase, which activates protein kinase G (PKG); this pathway ultimately inhibits sodium and water reabsorption at the renal collecting duct, promoting natriuresis and diuresis.
